Run cognitive interviews with language models playing personas

Source: R/interview.R
cognitive_interview.Rd

cognitive_interview() asks one or more language models to take part in a cognitive interview about each survey item, as each persona. It is meant for screening items when there are no real respondents yet, for example after a synthetic_pretest(): It points to wording to look at. It is not a substitute for cognitive interviews with real people or for a field test.

Usage

cognitive_interview(
  instrument,
  models,
  personas = NULL,
  items = NULL,
  probes = sc_probes(),
  coder = NULL,
  pretest = NULL,
  interviews = 1,
  max_retries = 2,
  parallel = 1,
  output = NULL,
  format = c("csv", "json", "rds"),
  progress = interactive(),
  progress_file = NULL,
  stop_file = NULL,
  seed = 1,
  cache = sc_cache()
)

Arguments

instrument

an sc_instrument().

models

one sc_model() or a list of them, the respondents.

personas

an sc_personas() table, a character vector of descriptions, or NULL for interviews without a persona.

items

optional item names to interview about. NULL uses all items, or only the flagged items when pretest is given.

probes

the probes, from sc_probes().

coder

an sc_model() that codes the transcripts. NULL uses each respondent model to code its own interviews. The coder's temperature is set to 0 when it takes one.

pretest

optional result of synthetic_pretest(), or a data frame with an item column and an optional flag column (the reason, for example "low item-rest correlation"), or a vector of item names. Flagged items come first and get one extra probe.

interviews

number of interviews per model, persona and item.

max_retries

how often to retry an interview that fails.

parallel

number of interviews to run at the same time.

output

optional folder to write the results to: The table in format, run.json, and one readable Markdown file of transcripts per item in transcripts/.

format

file format of the table in output: "csv", "json" or "rds".

progress

show a progress bar in the console? A function also works, as in generate_synthetic().

progress_file

optional path of a JSON file updated after every interview (used by run_synthcheck_app()).

stop_file

optional path: When this file appears, the run stops after the interviews in progress.

seed

random seed for the mock provider, also part of the cache key.

cache

the response cache, as in generate_synthetic(): An sc_cache(), a folder, TRUE or FALSE. The respondent's two answers and the coding are saved, so the same interviews again cost nothing.

Value

A tibble of class sc_interview, one row per model, persona, item and interview, with model, provider, model_id, coder, persona_id, any persona attributes, item, statement, pretest (the flag, if any), interview, answer, think_aloud, one probe_<probe_id> column per probe, one logical column per stage (comprehension, retrieval, judgement, response, sensitivity) with a <stage>_note beside it, severity ("none", "minor" or "major") and revision. The attribute log holds failed interviews. Summarise it with summarise_interviews() and plot it with gg_interview().

Details

Each interview is one conversation with one persona about one item, following the standard mix of think-aloud and scripted verbal probes (Willis, 2005; Beatty & Willis, 2007):

  1. Think-aloud and answer. The persona reads the statement, says what goes through its mind while deciding, and answers on the instrument's scale.

  2. Probes. The persona answers the probes in sc_probes() in the same conversation. Items flagged by the pretest get one more probe aimed at the reason for the flag.

  3. Coding. A separate call, with no persona, reads the transcript and codes problems at the four stages of answering a survey question (comprehension, retrieval, judgement, response mapping; Tourangeau, 1984) plus sensitivity, as in the Question Appraisal System (Willis & Lessler, 1999). For each stage it gives a yes or no, a short note with a quote, an overall severity and an optional rewording. Use another model as coder so that no model grades its own interviews.

That is three requests per interview. The number of interviews is the number of models times personas times items times interviews, and it is printed before the run starts.

What a model can and cannot tell you: A model does not retrieve memories or feel uncomfortable, so its retrieval and judgement reports are guesses about what such a person might say. Comprehension and response-mapping problems (vague or double-barrelled wording, a scale that fits poorly) are where it helps most. Models understand items better than many real respondents, so an item without problems here is not shown to work.

References

Beatty, P. C., & Willis, G. B. (2007). Research synthesis: The practice of cognitive interviewing. Public Opinion Quarterly, 71(2), 287-311.

Tourangeau, R. (1984). Cognitive science and survey methods. In T. Jabine, M. Straf, J. Tanur & R. Tourangeau (Eds.), Cognitive aspects of survey methodology: Building a bridge between disciplines (pp. 73-100). National Academy Press.

Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive interviewing: A tool for improving questionnaire design. Sage.

Willis, G. B., & Lessler, J. T. (1999). Question Appraisal System QAS-99. Research Triangle Institute.

See also

sc_probes(), summarise_interviews(), gg_interview(), sc_interview_prompts(), estimate_interview_cost(), sc_cache()

Examples

items <- data.frame(
  item = c("q1", "q2", "q3"),
  statement = c("I am not someone who never worries.",
                "I enjoy meeting new people and going to parties.",
                "I keep my promises."))
ins <- sc_instrument(items, scale = c(1, 5))
per <- sc_personas(c("You are a 19-year-old student.", "You are a 70-year-old retiree."))
iv <- cognitive_interview(ins, sc_model("mock"), per)
#> 6 interviews (1 model x 2 personas x 3 items): 18 requests.
iv
#> # A tibble: 6 × 29
#>   model provider model_id coder persona_id item  statement     pretest interview
#>   <chr> <chr>    <chr>    <chr> <chr>      <chr> <chr>         <chr>       <int>
#> 1 mock  mock     mock     mock  p001       q1    I am not som… NA              1
#> 2 mock  mock     mock     mock  p001       q2    I enjoy meet… NA              1
#> 3 mock  mock     mock     mock  p001       q3    I keep my pr… NA              1
#> 4 mock  mock     mock     mock  p002       q1    I am not som… NA              1
#> 5 mock  mock     mock     mock  p002       q2    I enjoy meet… NA              1
#> 6 mock  mock     mock     mock  p002       q3    I keep my pr… NA              1
#> # ℹ 20 more variables: answer <int>, think_aloud <chr>, probe_paraphrase <chr>,
#> #   probe_terms <chr>, probe_retrieval <chr>, probe_judgement <chr>,
#> #   probe_response <chr>, probe_sensitivity <chr>, comprehension <lgl>,
#> #   comprehension_note <chr>, retrieval <lgl>, retrieval_note <chr>,
#> #   judgement <lgl>, judgement_note <chr>, response <lgl>, response_note <chr>,
#> #   sensitivity <lgl>, sensitivity_note <chr>, severity <chr>, revision <chr>
summarise_interviews(iv)
#> 3 of 3 items are flagged: q1 (100% of interviews, mostly
#> comprehension); q2 (100% of interviews, mostly comprehension); q3 (50%
#> of interviews, mostly comprehension). These are screening results from
#> language models: Use them to choose items for cognitive interviews with
#> real people and a field test, not to replace them.
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 9
#>   item  comprehension retrieval judgement response sensitivity   any models
#>   <chr>         <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl> <dbl>  <int>
#> 1 q1              1         0         0          0           0   1        1
#> 2 q2              0.5       0.5       0.5        0           0   1        1
#> 3 q3              0.5       0         0          0           0   0.5      1
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: flagged <lgl>
if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY
iv <- cognitive_interview(ins, list(sc_model("anthropic"), sc_model("openai")), per,
                          coder = sc_model("anthropic"), parallel = 4)
} # }
